claims.text: A controlled increase in phosphorus content will enhance the alloy's glass-forming ability.
A controlled increase in phosphorus content will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Increasing phosphorus promotes local atomic motifs that frustrate crystallization.
The baseline alloy has moderate glass-forming ability and crystallizes at relatively low temperatures.
The intervention is a small, controlled increase in phosphorus content during alloy synthesis.
The intervention is expected to work under rapid-quenching conditions when complementary alloying elements do not overwhelm phosphorus-induced effects.
The intervention may not work when the alloy is already saturated with phosphorus or competing phase formation dominates.
Additional phosphorus enhances the formation of phosphorus-centered clusters or short-range-order motifs that are topologically incompatible with crystalline order.
Additional phosphorus increases atomic-size mismatch and chemical-bonding heterogeneity.
The increased atomic-size mismatch and bonding heterogeneity deepen the energy well for the amorphous phase.
Increased local structural frustration raises the activation energy for crystallization.
Raising the activation energy for crystallization expands the glass-forming range and stabilizes the amorphous state during heating.
The modified alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for vitrification than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will exhibit a higher crystallization peak temperature in DSC than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will exhibit improved thermal stability during isothermal annealing relative to the baseline alloy.
The benefit is limited to regimes in which phosphorus remains a minor additive.
Phosphorus additions beyond an optimal limit may cause phase separation or embrittlement.
The improvement depends on processing conditions that avoid kinetically controlled crystallization.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly permits detrimental phase separation or embrittlement when phosphorus exceeds an unspecified optimal limit, but the falsification rule treats occurrence of either feature during a systematic phosphorus increase as falsifying the hypothesis without restricting that criterion to the claimed beneficial minor-additive regime.
